newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Wary Swiss bankers play down Mobutu assets freeze.
newsitem.headline: Wary Swiss bankers play down Mobutu assets freeze.

text.p: Swiss bankers played down Berne's step to freeze assets that Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko and his family may have in Switzerland, insisting on Tuesday that dictators with fortunes to hide had moved them long ago.
The seizure of any Mobutu family wealth in Switzerland was a politically necessary step that helps dispel the country's past image as silent guardian of ill-gotten gains, they added.

But they disagreed on whether it could also scare away other banking customers concerned that Switzerland's vaunted tradition of banking secrecy was wilting, a perception that could in the long run drive business to other offshore financial centres.

"I don't think this will have a big impact," said Heinrich Schneider, deputy secretary general of the Swiss Bankers Association, calling the weekend step a foreign policy decision that simply cemented banking regulators' clampdown last week.
After Berne's blockage of Ferdinand Marcos' millions after the Philippines president was ousted, it should come as no surprise that Switzerland will act when needed, he said.
"Anyone who is just realising this now is in any event a badly informed money stasher," he said.

Michel Derobert, secretary general of the Swiss Private Bankers Association in Geneva, agreed the publicity surrounding Mobutu's money may discourage shadowy figures from bringing money to Switzerland.
But he said the issue was unlikely to have any impact on the vaunted private banking business.

"We're not really concerned about this issue. I'm not sure there is any money, if Mr Mobutu has any sense after what happened to Marcos," he said, stressing Swiss banks do everything they can to avoid taking questionable money.
Another banker who asked not to be identified said Berne's willingness to seize dubious bank accounts could scare away some rich clients seeking absolute secrecy for their wealth.

"The danger may exist that this constant softening or hollowing out of banking secrecy may make some people feel they cannot expect the same discretion that they had hoped for. It is hard to judge what kind of impact this may have," he said.
Customers afraid of getting tangled in the law or in banks' internal controls know that "there are certainly other financial centres where this danger is not as great", he added.
But Schneider scoffed at such talk.
"Anyone who is smart knows that nothing about banking secrecy has changed in any way or is being applied or interpreted differently, although people often say this," he said.

Jean Ziegler, a Socialist member of parliament and author who is one of Swiss banks' most outspoken critics, said he believed Mobutu had several billion dollars in the country and slammed Berne for dragging its heels.
"The Swiss government should have ordered the blockage months ago. The government's move was much too late," he told Reuters, adding he thought banks would now try to shield Mobutu.

"Swiss bankers will try to protect Mobutu because if they let him down, this would be a signal to all other African dictators and shadowy figures not to bring their money to Switzerland," he said. "The banks are caught in between."
